subtype: Changing an answer after others answer [Actor]
passage: "What is eight times seven?" asked Ms Iyer. "Fifty-four!" called half the class. "Fifty-four," said Keerthana, firmly. Uma's pencil hovered over the number she had written. "Uma?" "Um... fifty-four?" "Are you sure?" Ms Iyer's eyebrows lifted. Uma stared at her notebook. "Fifty-six is what I wrote," Uma mumbled, "but everyone said..." Rohan, at the back, had said nothing at all. "Thank you for telling us, Uma. Class, let us count in eights together." Keerthana's ears went red.

qa.q: What number had Uma written in her notebook?
What was Uma thinking when saying fifty-four aloud?
qa.a: Uma doubted the written answer because most of the class said something else; agreeing felt easier than being the lone voice, even though Uma privately had fifty-six.

qa.q: What could Uma try next time when the class says something different from an answer Uma is sure about?
qa.a: Uma could say "I got fifty-six, can we check?" or show the working, so the answer is tested rather than dropped.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel when Ms Iyer suggests counting in eights?
qa.a: Keerthana may feel embarrassed; going red suggests she was sure and has now been shown wrong in front of everyone.

grounding: A child who knew the right answer changes it when most of the class says otherwise, because self-doubt feels easier than being the lone voice.

subtype: Changing an answer after others answer [Actor]
passage: My name is Sharmila and this is about the day I changed a right answer. Sir asked, "Is a bat a bird or a mammal?" I knew it was a mammal because we had read about it. But Urmila said bird, and then most hands went up for bird. I lifted my hand for bird too. My tummy felt heavy. Only Kabir kept his hand still and said nothing. Later Sir told us it was a mammal and I wanted to hide under the desk. Urmila laughed at herself, but I did not laugh. I had known, and I let the others decide.

qa.q: What did the teacher ask about the bat?
qa.a: Sir asked whether a bat is a bird or a mammal.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila raise a hand for bird?
qa.a: Because most of the class chose bird, Sharmila trusted the crowd over private knowledge; the heavy tummy shows an uneasy, doubting feeling.

qa.q: What might Sharmila try at the moment the hands go up?
qa.a: Sharmila could keep the hand down or say "I read that it is a mammal", giving the class a second answer to think about.

qa.q: What might Kabir have been feeling by keeping a hand still and saying nothing?
qa.a: Kabir may have been unsure, or sure and afraid of speaking up; not joining the bird hands suggests unwillingness to follow the crowd without knowing.

grounding: A child who knew the right answer changes it after others answer, feeling heavy afterwards for letting the group decide.
